title: What's the deal with crash testing?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and practice of automotive crash testing. They cover GM's 1934 barrier test at Milford Proving Ground, Sam Alderson and Alderson Research Laboratories creating Sierra Sam and the Hybrid III dummy, and the shift from the fiftieth percentile male dummy to the fifth percentile female (H3-5F). They discuss sensors and paint-marked dummies, post-mortem human subjects, and how NHTSA and the IIHS run tests (full frontal, offset, side, pole, and small overlap) with star ratings and the Abbreviated Injury Scale. They also cover how crash testing drove airbags, pretensioners, force limiters, and side curtains, the push toward virtual simulation, and criticisms about test speeds and mismatched vehicles. The episode ends with a listener letter about a craniotomy and trepanning.

segments.title: Opening banter and overview of car crash safety
segments.summary: Hosts check whether the show has covered crash testing before, then outline how modern cars are designed to protect occupants and how crash testing pushed automakers toward safety.

segments.title: History of crash testing and early dummies
segments.summary: GM held the first barrier test in 1934 at Milford Proving Ground. Sam Alderson's company later created Sierra Sam, the first crash test dummy, and the Hybrid III line followed.

segments.title: Dummy size standards and representation
segments.summary: The fiftieth percentile male dummy was used for decades. Testers now use the fifth percentile female dummy, and some are adding child and obese dummies. A bill from Eleanor Holmes Norton would require female dummies.

segments.title: Limits of dummies and post-mortem human subjects
segments.summary: Dummies cannot replicate tissue damage and are built for repeated use. Some testing uses embalmed and fresh post-mortem human subjects. Automakers also run internal crash tests before regulatory testing.

segments.title: Sensors, paint marks, and simulation
segments.summary: Dummies carry accelerometers and load and movement sensors. Body parts are painted to show contact points. The hosts discuss biofidelic dummies and a future shift toward computer simulation.

segments.title: How IIHS and NHTSA run tests
segments.summary: Test cars are prepped by replacing fluids with mineral spirits and weighing them. Dummies are seated, cameras are set up, and cars are pulled on a track into barriers. Tests include full frontal and offset impacts, and the IIHS tests at 40 mph versus 35 mph for NHTSA.

segments.title: Small overlap tests, injury scales, and star ratings
segments.summary: The IIHS added overlap tests after finding corner impacts were dangerous. The Abbreviated Injury Scale is used for injury classification. NHTSA and IIHS rating systems changed in 2011 and 2010, with cars now compared against each other.

segments.title: Safety features driven by crash testing
segments.summary: Pretensioners, force limiters, airbags, and side curtain airbags came from crash testing. Side curtains were added for pole impacts. The hosts also discuss mismatched vehicle crashes, test speeds, and speeding drivers.

segments.title: Listener mail about craniotomy and trepanning
segments.summary: Amanda writes that she had a craniotomy for Chiari malformation and connects it to the trepanning episode, including the claim that surgery was discussed as a depression treatment.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the listener email address and sign off.
